ABO: A Gaussian Ashfall Model and Interactive Eruption Laboratory for 
Philippine Volcanoes  
BSCS 4B | CSE 103 - Computational Science 
11 October 2026 
Abstract 
ABO is a local computational science application for examining how eruption inputs, wind and 
prescribed settling speeds influence ground ash deposition around Taal, Mayon and Kanlaon. 
This study developed and evaluated a reduced analytical Gaussian fallout model implemented 
in Python and presented through a React interface. The model integrates deposits exactly over 
rectangular cells, samples municipal centroids, evaluates 360 wind directions and computes 
accumulation during and after a finite period of constant ash emission. Geographic three-
dimensional illustrations and an optional terrain-guided lava teaching model provide additional 
context. Evaluation combined independent synthetic references, conservation and coordinate 
checks, data-provenance audits and browser workflows. Verification passed 142 Python cases, 
alongside frontend regression and build checks. A saved illustrative Mayon request emitted 
36,000,000 kg of ash; 30,459,336.29 kg deposited within the model domain and 5,540,663.71 
kg outside it after complete settling. These values are computational results of assumed inputs, 
not observations of a Mayon eruption. A frozen Taal retrospective protocol rejected both 
candidate soundings for insufficient altitude coverage. Two independent traces of a published 
contour agreed closely, but shared source dependence and missing physical inputs prevented 
predictive evaluation. ABO supports reproducible educational exploration and point-exposure 
screening; historical accuracy and damage assessments remain unestablished. 
Keywords: volcanic ashfall; Gaussian fallout; finite emission; municipal screening; scientific 
visualization 
1. Introduction 
Volcanic ash deposition affects communities through ground loading and disruption of 
infrastructure and agriculture. Philippine eruptions motivate locally interpretable tools: Balangue-
Tarriela et al. (2022) documented the January 2020 Taal fallout using crowdsourced information 
and field observations. Building impacts depend on deposit characteristics, structural design 
and environmental conditions rather than one universal thickness limit (U.S. Geological Survey 
[USGS], 2015). A computational tool should therefore distinguish calculated deposition from 
evidence of damage. 
Analytical tephra models provide a practical basis for exploring transport and settling. Tephra2 
estimates accumulated tephra mass using eruption and particle inputs and allows wind to vary 
with height (Geoscience Community Codes, n.d.). ABO adopts the general analytical advection-
diffusion approach but uses a simpler release distribution, one effective horizontal wind and 
prescribed settling speeds. Its equations and implementation are defined independently; 
equivalence to the complete Tephra2 model is not claimed.

2 
The study aimed to develop a reproducible Python and React application that links explicit 
physical assumptions to maps, centroid samples and three-dimensional teaching illustrations. It 
addressed three questions: whether the reduced model preserves its analytical and mass-
accounting properties; whether the interface presents consistent quantities and unavailable 
evidence; and what additional information is required before the application can support 
historical evaluation. The initial proposal's broader aspirations for seasonal presets, Taal 
replication and impact thresholds are treated as requirements whose scientific completion must 
be demonstrated. 
The study covers a regional flat-ground ash model, a finite-emission extension, municipal point 
screening, wind-direction comparison and a separate Mayon lava teaching model. It excludes a 
solved buoyant eruption column, airborne gas or ash concentration, rainfall removal, 
aggregation, pyroclastic density currents, lahars and building-specific assessment. Its 
geographic illustrations improve orientation without supplying these omitted processes. 
2. Methods 
2.1 Study design, application and source records 
The study used computational model development and verification. No participant study or field 
sampling was conducted. Python, FastAPI, NumPy, SciPy, pyproj and Shapely supply 
validation, numerical arrays and spatial operations. React, Three.js and React Three Fiber 
present backend results; Leaflet displays geographic layers. Python remains the authority for 
computed quantities and response contracts. The application runs locally on Windows, and 
simulations use manually curated local scientific records rather than live weather or eruption 
APIs. 
The catalog contains three volcano profiles, 318 municipal/city records with 2024 populations 
and two airport reference points. Municipal records use unique Philippine Standard Geographic 
Code identifiers and equal-area centroids derived from simplified geoBoundaries administrative 
polygons. Population values are transcribed from Philippine Statistics Authority (PSA, n.d.) 
directories, with source snapshots and census years retained. Official 2020 counts are also 
recorded for 34 Batangas jurisdictions, with documented administrative-code crosswalks; the 
other 284 historical counts remain unavailable. Volcano coordinates and reference elevations 
follow Smithsonian Global Volcanism Program (n.d.) profiles. 
The coverage audit identifies administrative polygons intersecting each fixed simulation square, 
including unresolved name/code matches. Taal includes 162 of 214 intersecting records, Mayon 
37 of 112, and Kanlaon 109 of 171; the remainder are explicitly unresolved. These domain 
totals overlap and must not be summed as unique jurisdictions. Twenty-three included domain 
records have their centroids outside the relevant square, so their point predictions remain 
unknown even though part of the polygon intersects it. A centroid represents one sample, not 
every location in a municipality. The inventory remains partial rather than complete national or 
domain coverage. 
Static geographic assets combine Mapzen Skadi elevation, Natural Earth land and lakes, and a 
cached OpenStreetMap Taal Lake polygon with its island holes (Mapzen, n.d.; Natural Earth,

3 
n.d.; OpenStreetMap contributors, n.d.). Each volcano backdrop spans 100 by 100 km with 250 
m display samples. Horizontal coordinates are WGS84 and elevations use the EGM96 geoid. 
Raw Mayon elevation also supports the separate lava route. Historic terrain and generalized 
shorelines are not current crater surveys. Source identifiers, units, conversions, dates, hashes 
and interpretation limits are retained in the project registry. 
2.2 Coordinates, inputs and assumptions 
A vent-centered azimuthal-equidistant projection expresses east and north distances in metres. 
Geographic transformations explicitly use longitude before latitude. The ash grid spans 200 by 
200 km with 1 km cells: 200 rows and 200 columns. Model ground is flat at the submitted vent 
datum. A plume height reported above sea level must be reduced by that datum before being 
used as height above model ground. The published Taal height range of 17-21 km above sea 
level consequently cannot be entered as an unconverted above-ground value (Balangue-
Tarriela et al., 2022). 
Ash emission is constant for the specified duration. Horizontal wind is uniform, diffusion is 
isotropic, class settling speeds are constant and the default release distribution has 16 equally 
weighted midpoint heights. Grain fractions sum to one. Bulk deposit density converts 
accumulated load to thickness; it is distinct from particle density. Representative diameters label 
the classes but do not determine their terminal speeds in this implementation.

below are teaching assumptions, not event measurements.

uE = −U sin(f);   uN = −U cos(f).   (2)

5 
Receptor loads use Equation 4 directly. Deposit thickness is dmm = 1000 L/ρbulk, where ρbulk is in 
kg/m³. Mass inside the finite square and mass outside it are reported separately; the grid is not 
renormalized to conceal loss beyond its extent. 
2.4 Finite emission and eruption illustrations 
At observation time t, material released at time b arrives after b + τij. Integrating constant 
emission over 0 ≤ b ≤ T gives the arrived component mass: 
Aij(t) =

Substituting Aij(t) for final component mass in Equations 4 and 5 computes accumulated 
deposition. Emitted mass is Q min(t,T); still-aloft mass is emitted mass minus arrived mass. 
Arrived mass splits into inside-domain and outside-domain deposits. Complete accumulation 
occurs at T + max(τij), over every class and layer, rather than when emission stops. 
The default response contains 37 snapshots, with nonuniform spacing during emission and its 
fallout tail. Requests whose extreme values cannot maintain the requested distinct clock 
samples are rejected. Python supplies representative airborne centers and spreads from the 
surviving age intervals; React interpolates supplied geometry and renders enlarged billows. 
Source rise, condensed-steam appearance and prescribed Taal fountain arcs are illustrations 
rather than solved buoyancy, condensation or ballistic hazards. Taal close-up relief is enlarged 
sixfold and fountain geometry fourfold, with visible labels; regional terrain scale returns to one-
to-one. 
2.5 Terrain-guided lava teaching model 
An optional Mayon demonstration routes one channel down the steepest positive drop among 
eight DEM neighbors. The route uses raw elevations and actual diagonal distances. Its fluid is 
isothermal, laminar and Newtonian. The mean-speed relation follows the Jeffreys expression 
discussed by Borch et al. (2025):

Here q is effusion in m³/s, w channel width in metres, h depth normal to the inclined channel in 
metres, ρl lava density in kg/m³, η dynamic viscosity in Pa·s and α slope angle. The computation 
adopts gravitational acceleration g = 9.80665 m/s². The teaching inputs are q = 5 m³/s, w = 20 
m, η = 1,000 Pa·s and ρl = 2,600 kg/m³. These values are assumed and are independent of ash 
inputs. Travel time uses inclined segment length divided by mean velocity, and volume uses 
width times normal depth times inclined length. 
Routing stops at water, a flat or pit, the asset edge, the declared horizontal distance cap or the 
effusion-duration limit. Current-time footprints use the prescribed width; the visible ribbon is 
enlarged separately. The implementation does not represent cooling, crystallization, yield 
strength, branching, constriction backup, pond filling or surface changes. General lava-flow 
controls described by USGS (n.d.) and the dated Mayon bulletin (Philippine Institute of

6 
Volcanology and Seismology [PHIVOLCS], 2023) provide context, not calibration of this route or 
its material values. 
2.6 Screening, wind sweep and evaluation 
The default 0.5 mm contour defines a reporting footprint, not a damage threshold. Receptor 
comparisons use greater-than-or-equal thresholds. Conditional screening requires a reviewed 
criterion, an explicitly supported receptor type and matching conditions selected for the scenario 
or recorded for that receptor. An absent type, condition or applicability basis returns unknown 
with a reason. A municipal roof or crop context is a conditional scenario, not a survey of local 
buildings or crops. Missing damage criteria or outside-domain receptors retain unknown status. 
Indicative population totals deduplicate municipality identifiers; whole municipal populations 
selected by a centroid are not people counted inside a deposit polygon. Airport and water-facility 
results describe surface deposition only, not airborne aviation safety or water potability. 
Population years are selected explicitly; a missing 2020 value cannot be replaced with a 2024 
count. 
The sweep evaluates bearings from 0 through 359 degrees at one-degree intervals directly at 
receptors, holding all other inputs fixed. Each receptor receives its maximum load and 
corresponding wind-from bearing, with exact ties resolved to the lowest angle. These individual 
maxima form an envelope across different scenarios, not one simultaneous regional deposit. 
Verification used independent scalar expectations, zero-mass and calm-wind cases, cardinal 
bearings, projection round trips, finite nonnegative outputs, threshold equality, cell-resolution 
comparisons, release-layer sensitivity, timeline monotonicity, final-state agreement, lava travel 
and volume, invalid local terrain and preallocation resource bounds. Browser checks traced 
completed results through stages, selectors, point inspection, map labels, exports and 
responsive themes. Memory is conservatively bounded at 512 MiB and concurrent calculations 
are limited. 
Historical evaluation requires dated event inputs and independent geolocated observations with 
uncertainty. Calibration and evaluation samples must be separate. The implemented 
comparison reports signed interval residuals, midpoint residuals, interval-distance RMSE and 
MAE, midpoint RMSE and MAE, coverage and grid-center footprint intersection-over-union 
within the modeled domain. The compatibility field rmsemm denotes interval-distance RMSE. For 
a reported interval [a,b], an interval residual is p-a below a, p-b above b, and zero inside the 
interval; midpoint error instead compares p with (a+b)/2. Per-observation records retain 
coordinates, split, dependency group and outside-domain reasons. A scalar isopach area 
cannot establish spatial overlap. Numerical verification, input readiness and historical 
assessment remain separate statuses. 
2.7 Frozen retrospective protocol and public wind evidence 
The first retrospective target is the mapped Taal main-plume fallout from 12 January 2020 at 
13:00 to 13 January at 04:28 Philippine Standard Time, equivalent to 05:00-20:28 UTC on 12 
January, or 55,680 s. Protocol taal-main-plume-2020-v1 and dataset taal-published-evidence-v1 
were frozen before model agreement was calculated. The study also uses an approximately

7 
04:00 endpoint for a figure and a narrower intense-plume period. Its transition to lava 
fountaining at 02:49 is another event definition. These intervals are preserved separately; the 
mapped interval is not treated as a measured period of constant emission. The Smithsonian 
profile elevation of 311 m is not established as the historical active-vent datum. 
The parameter register classifies measured, derived, calibrated and assumed values and 
retains units, datum, uncertainty, source locator, license, conversions and dependencies. 
Deposit-derived volume, inferred plume height, thickness observations and contours from the 
same study share a dependency family. Distal samples do not independently establish the 
emitted grain spectrum. Ash mass and bulk deposit density cannot be identified separately from 
thickness alone because their ratio sets the amplitude. 
NOAA IGRA 2.2 station RPM00098433 at Tanay was chosen as the public sounding candidate. 
The selected nominal 00:00 and 12:00 UTC launches on 12 January were archived with their 
actual release times, raw fields and source hashes. Missing or removed values are rejected; 
wind speed in tenths of m/s is converted to m/s, height processing flags are retained and no 
nonexistent independent wind-quality flag is invented. Meteorological wind-from bearings are 
converted to east and north components before averaging. Each profile is interpolated onto a 
fixed 1 km geopotential-height grid from 1 to 21 km ASL, only within observed coverage. The 
frozen rule requires at least 75% of these 21 heights. Accepted heights and launches would 
receive equal weights; a resultant below 0.1 m/s would have no assigned direction. Station 
distance, launch offsets, shear and altitude conventions remain representativeness limitations 
(NOAA National Centers for Environmental Information [NCEI], n.d.). 
Independent eruption inputs are preferred, with all deposit measurements held out. If calibration 
becomes necessary, only diffusivity and initial spread are eligible under this protocol. A 
deterministic 70% calibration and 30% evaluation split operates on complete spatial groups, 
rounding down the calibration count and retaining at least one evaluation group. Duplicate 
coordinates and shared measurements remain together. A dependency family is confined to 
one partition or excluded from an independent-point claim. Interpolated contour vertices do not 
become additional independent observations. The split is frozen before fitting and evaluation 
observations cannot guide parameter tuning. 
Contour-derived evidence requires two independent traces, documented georeferencing 
residuals and measured inter-trace disagreement. Two digitizers independently froze pixel 
traces of the published Figure 4a outer 0.05 cm contour before comparing coordinates or model 
outputs. The source PDF, XML, image and metadata were archived through the official NIH 
PMC open-data archive, retaining hashes and the article's CC BY 4.0 license. Separate affine 
fits translate printed longitude/latitude ticks into coordinates, assuming WGS84 because the 
original map datum is unspecified. WGS84 geodesic areas and a vent-centered azimuthal-
equidistant overlay quantify repeatability and clipping. Both traces belong to the same 
dependent source family, with zero independent point observations (Balangue-Tarriela et al., 
2022; National Library of Medicine [NLM], n.d.). 
The source's fitting assumptions of 10% thickness/diameter and 20% distal-limit error do not 
establish a complete ABO predictive tolerance. Without accepted spatial uncertainty and 
independent physical inputs, any comparison is descriptive and validation remains

8 
unestablished. Planned sensitivity includes 0.5, 1 and 2 km cells, 8, 16 and 32 release layers 
and source-supported input endpoints without refitting. No empirical fit was authorized while 
those evidence gates remained blocked. 
3. Results 
3.1 Analytical and software verification 
The full Python verification passed 142 cases, including 23 new independent gap-closure cases, 
12 new implementation provenance/readiness cases and the previously recorded 107 cases. All 
56 frontend regression cases, lint, type checking and production build also passed. Earlier two-
agent review identified nine numerical, timing, terrain, provenance and presentation findings. 
The current independent review additionally found a wind-average bearing wrapping to 360 
degrees and a negative population record causing a server error; normalization and input 
validation corrected both, with passing independent retests. New cases cover source coverage, 
datum conversion, grouped leakage, conditional applicability, historical census selection and 
separate interval/midpoint metrics, including valid counterexamples. Test counts demonstrate 
the tested behavior, not statistical prediction accuracy. 
A synthetic calm-wind reference used Q = 100 kg/s, T = 1,000 s, K = 0, σ0 = 1,000 m and ρbulk = 
1,000 kg/m³, with three classes sharing equal settling speed. Its total mass was 100,000 kg. 
Analytical point load at the vent was 0.0159154943 kg/m² and thickness was 0.0159154943 
mm. Exact mass in the centered 1 km square was 14,663.1496308 kg, yielding 0.0146631496 
kg/m² cell-average load. The difference between point and area-average values was expected 
and independently tested. 
3.2 Reproducible teaching example 
The saved Mayon sequence request used Tables 1 and 2 and returned 37 snapshots. With the 
highest release midpoint at 4,843.75 m and slowest settling speed 0.05 m/s, the maximum 
falling time was 96,875 s. Adding 3,600 s of emission gave a final arrival time of 100,475 s, or 
about 1,674.6 min. A fresh local API run produced the final mass accounting in Table 3. This 
example tests a stated scenario; it does not reconstruct a measured eruption. 
Table 3. Final ash mass accounting for the saved illustrative Mayon request. 
Quantity Mass (kg) Interpretation 
Emitted ash 36,000,000.00 Rate multiplied by duration 
Deposited inside domain 30,459,336.29 Exact integrated mass in the 200 km 
square 
Deposited outside domain 5,540,663.71 Arrived ash beyond the finite square 
Still aloft 0.00 Complete modeled settling 
 
Inside-domain and outside-domain mass summed to emitted mass at full settling. The lava route 
ended at its effusion-volume limit. This stop describes the prescribed channel calculation, not 
observed runout or a radius of safety.

9 
3.3 Data, interface and historical status 
Independent cached-source audits reproduced all 318 included 2024 population/code pairs and 
the 34 Batangas 2020 pairs, and independently recomputed domain intersections and 
unresolved coverage. Earlier terrain checks covered 17 source hashes, four output hashes, 
independent elevation samples and source-water samples. These results support local 
transcription and asset reproducibility within the included inventory, rather than complete 
domain coverage or reviewed physical presets. 
Browser workflows displayed the shared sequence beside the effect map, with explicit snapshot 
quantities and separately labeled eventual table totals. The 320 px layouts remained within the 
viewport in both themes. Final production-build timing used the Mayon teaching preset with lava 
enabled, close-up camera, normal detail, a 1,440 × 1,000 viewport and pixel ratio 1 on a Ryzen 
7 5800U / Radeon machine. After one warm-up, three complete replays yielded minimum 
steady 10-second rates of 51.2, 59.4 and 59.8 rendered frames per second in Chrome, and 
58.5, 58.7 and 58.9 in the in-app browser. Raw callbacks and rendered timestamps were 
retained. Sampled OS foreground ownership and page focus were confirmed. Two Chrome 
replays overlapped an earlier in-app warm-up; the subsequent in-app campaign was sequential. 
These measurements replace the earlier one-frame-per-second Chrome observation for this 
build and setup, without establishing a universal performance guarantee. 
A 1,823.6-second resource soak completed 20 volcano/run/view cycles and 38 full replays 
without JavaScript errors. All 38 sampled paused windows rendered zero additional frames. 
After corrections to shared graphics-resource listeners and retired renderer wrappers, post-
collection heap grew from 29.45 MiB after the first cycle to 35.93 MiB after cycle 20, then 59.69 
MiB at the end. DOM nodes and event-listener counts rose during repeated view cycles and 
subsequently stabilized; the full cleanup gate remains open. The soak disabled background 
throttling for resource continuity and is separate from the foreground performance 
measurement. Reduced-motion changes and graphics failures received targeted browser tests. 
A real hidden-page transition, native browser 200% zoom, screen-reader speech and Word's 
native accessibility checker remain unestablished; CSS zoom and accessibility-tree checks 
provide narrower evidence. 
Historical Taal agreement remained unavailable. The source review preserved the published 
8,605 km² narrative footprint and the locally curated Table 3 entry of 3,864.89 km² at 0.05 cm, 
equivalent to 0.5 mm (Balangue-Tarriela et al., 2022). The differing entries were not silently 
reconciled or used to invent overlap metrics. No empirical thickness error, validated footprint 
agreement or forecast accuracy is reported. 
3.4 Wind-coverage result and descriptive sensitivity 
The archived Tanay profiles were released at 00:11 and 11:40 UTC on 12 January 2020. Each 
retained nine levels with usable height and wind data, spanning approximately 1.5-16.6 km ASL. 
Interpolation covered the 2-16 km grid heights: 15 of 21, or 71.43%. Both failed the frozen 75% 
coverage requirement. Their effective historical wind remains unavailable; the coverage 
threshold was not relaxed after seeing the records. Figure 1 shows the retained components

10 
without extrapolation. These data document an unsuccessful source-coverage gate, not a failed 
model prediction. 
 
Figure 1. Archived Tanay wind components on 12 January 2020. Circles/solid lines 
identify 00:11 UTC and squares/dashed lines 11:40 UTC. Positive components point east 
or north. The lines connect retained levels for inspection, rather than supplying winds 
above the observed range. Source: NOAA IGRA 2.2, RPM00098433; processing and 
source hashes are retained locally. 
An initial publisher-image acquisition returned a browser-challenge HTML response under an 
image filename. It was rejected before tracing. Subsequent retrieval from the official PMC open-
data archive supplied the actual source PDF and image. The two independently frozen traces 
yield geodesic areas of 8,639.95 and 8,656.14 km², a 0.187% relative difference. Their vent-
projection intersection-over-union is 0.97918 and their boundary Hausdorff distance is 
approximately 1.90 km. An independent equal-area projection check gives an IoU of 0.97918 
and a 1.84 km boundary distance; the distance depends on the comparison projection. These 
are source-digitization comparisons, not prediction metrics. 
The scientific trace has approximately 108 m control-point RMSE and a 554 m declared pixel-
reading bound. The QA trace records axis control residuals of 0.283 and 0.214 pixels and a 983 
m tracing/quantization bound. These bounds describe each digitizer's procedure rather than a 
common confidence interval. Original field, interpolation, erosion, datum and event-window 
uncertainties remain additional and unquantified. Approximately 4.98% and 4.88% of the 
projected trace areas lie outside the model square. Model overlap must therefore use clipped 
geometry and disclose the omitted portion.

11 
Both traces are near the published 8,605 km² narrative area and differ substantially from the 
Table 3 value of 3,864.89 km². Neither trace was adjusted to either number; the publication's 
differing definitions remain unresolved. Independent ash mass, bulk density, emitted grain 
spectrum and historical active-vent datum also remain blocked. No model-observation residual 
or predictive IoU figure is reported. The historical interface exposes both derived contours, their 
uncertainty and dependencies, the protocol, input readiness and assessment reasons. 
 
Figure 2. Independent manual traces of the same published Figure 4a outer contour. 
Solid and dashed lines identify the digitizers; neither line represents an ABO prediction. 
Coordinates assume WGS84 from the printed graticule. Source: Balangue-Tarriela et al. 
(2022), archived through PMC, CC BY 4.0; derived geometry and source hashes are 
retained locally. 
Figure 3 reports a separate synthetic sensitivity calculation for the saved Mayon teaching inputs. 
At a fixed point 50 km northeast of the vent, the baseline thickness is 0.0269095 mm. Changing 
wind speed or column height individually from 80% to 120% of its assumed value changes the 
point prediction nonmonotonically as the finite release-height mixture moves past the receptor. 
The perturbations illustrate model dependence; they are neither source-supported confidence 
limits nor Taal residuals. The scalar Equation 4 calculations and figure input hashes are 
reproducible from the saved request.

12 
 
Figure 3. Synthetic point sensitivity of the Mayon teaching example, holding other inputs 
fixed and retaining 16 release layers. Circles identify wind speed; squares identify 
column height. The horizontal range is a teaching perturbation rather than a measured 
uncertainty interval. 
Independent reproduction matched all ten plotted thickness values to the NumPy solver within 
3.47e-18 mm. However, the same fixed-point thickness was 0.0411144, 0.0269095 and 
0.0318280 mm with 8, 16 and 32 release layers, respectively. The 18.28% increase from 16 to 
32 layers does not establish local release-height convergence. Corresponding inside-domain 
masses were approximately 30.36134, 30.45934 and 30.47728 million kg, showing that stable 
integrated mass does not imply stable point prediction. Exact cell integration at 0.5, 1 and 2 km 
gave the same domain mass and analytic receptor value; it cannot remove this separate 
release-height approximation. 
4. Discussion 
4.1 Meaning of the verified results 
The implemented model connects explicit parameters to accumulated ground load, thickness, 
sampled locations and reproducible exports. Exact cell integration and separate domain-loss 
accounting make conservation visible. The finite-emission extension explains why ash continues 
settling after the source stops, while the shared clock lets learners inspect changes without a 
second browser solver. Correct handling of wind-from bearings and sweep ties prevents 
presentation errors from becoming misleading directional conclusions. 
The three-dimensional scene supplies geographic and process context. Its recognizable land, 
water, source column and representative paths can support explanation, but scene realism is 
not independent evidence of model correctness. Enlarged Taal relief, fountain fragments, lava

13 
ribbons and qualitative billows have different roles from quantitative map thickness. Likewise, a 
dated PHIVOLCS reference zone concerns hazards beyond the implemented processes and 
cannot be treated as a current advisory or a simulated circular footprint. 
4.2 Scientific and evaluation limitations 
The ash assumptions omit changing wind, vertical shear, aggregation, wet deposition and 
terrain interception. Effective wind, release distribution and settling speed can strongly change 
transport distance. Constant-source timing does not reconstruct variable eruption pulses. 
Numeric agreement with the chosen equations therefore establishes computational consistency 
within the simplified model, not agreement with the complex event described by Balangue-
Tarriela et al. (2022). 
The lava model assumes a single fixed-width channel and constant rheology. It cannot 
reproduce the flow backup studied by Borch et al. (2025), cooling-dependent motion or 
branching inundation. Historic 250 m elevation sampling also limits local route detail. A stopped 
route denotes unknown continuation under omitted processes. Roof, crop and water impacts 
require condition-specific evidence, while ground airport screening cannot establish airborne 
exposure. 
Simplified boundary centroids and whole administrative population counts are unsuitable 
substitutes for a spatial population distribution. Missing census-year values and unresolved 
jurisdiction crosswalks remain visible rather than receiving newer or neighboring values. 
Software fixtures and browser layouts provide bounded evidence. No learner-effectiveness 
study was conducted. Controlled replay, lifecycle and accessibility findings are recorded 
separately from numerical and scientific status; unavailable screen-reader evidence cannot be 
replaced by an automated accessibility scan. 
4.3 Requirements for historical evaluation 
Event-specific evaluation requires ash mass or mass rate with duration, a consistent column-
height datum, dated plume-level wind by altitude and time, grain fractions, settling evidence, 
diffusion, initial spread and measured bulk deposit density. Reviewed seasonal winds must 
include altitude, region and averaging period; season names alone do not establish historical 
transport. Damage screening additionally needs roof categories, crop stages and facility-specific 
exposure criteria. 
Taal evaluation requires geolocated thickness measurements or accepted double-digitized 
contours with uncertainty and an event window, plus independent inputs or a disclosed grouped 
calibration/evaluation partition. The preserved footprint-area statements must be interpreted 
against their own geometry rather than selecting an area to match the model. The reviewed 
Tanay records do not reach the frozen altitude-coverage requirement; an alternative source or 
revised protocol would need prospective review and a new identity. Historical populations are 
selected by year and remain unknown where a 2020 source/crosswalk is unresolved. Lava 
evaluation separately needs dated vent/topography, effusion history, rheology, cooling and 
observed channel or inundation geometry. Until these are available, unavailable status is a 
scientifically meaningful result.

14 
4.4 Conclusion 
ABO provides a reproducible educational implementation of reduced Gaussian fallout, finite-
emission accumulation, centroid screening and interactive geographic illustration. Analytical 
checks and software tests support the implemented calculations and tested workflows. They do 
not establish calibrated eruption predictions, historical Taal agreement or condition-specific 
damage. The application is appropriate for examining stated assumptions and computational 
relationships while the remaining scientific evidence is collected and evaluated.
